title: [round · platform shape] Ten billion documents, fifty milliseconds
body:
> **Simulated interview round.** The shape a large-scale search or platform panel runs.

## The prompt

> *"Rank ten billion documents against a query in under fifty milliseconds. Walk me down the stack —
> from the inverted index to the cache line."*

## What this shape is testing

Whether you can reason about **what the big-O hides**. At this scale the constants *are* the design,
and a candidate who says "it's O(log n) so it's fine" has not built one.

## The staging, and the arithmetic at each stage

```text
10^10 docs
  |  stage 0  shard + route            ~200 shards, query hits all
  |  stage 1  posting-list intersect   10^10 -> 10^5   skip lists, WAND
  |  stage 2  cheap scoring            10^5  -> 10^3   BM25, no model
  |  stage 3  ANN / learned            10^3  -> 10^2
  |  stage 4  cross-encoder            10^2  -> 10^1   the only place a model can afford to run
```

**The whole game is the funnel.** Fifty milliseconds buys roughly one model call over ~100
documents. Everything above stage 4 exists to make those 100 the right 100.

## The follow-ups they will actually ask

**"Why is your posting list sorted by document id and not by score?"** Because intersecting sorted
lists is a merge, and score order destroys the property that makes it linear. Score-sorted lists
serve single-term queries, which are not the hard case.

**"Where does the cache line come in?"** Posting lists are compressed and decoded in blocks. A skip
pointer jumping outside the current cache line costs a memory round trip — ~100ns against ~1ns of
arithmetic. At 10^5 candidates that is the difference between 10ms and the whole budget.

**"What breaks first as you add filters?"** WAND's upper-bound pruning assumes it can skip
documents whose maximum possible score is below the threshold. A filter not in the index means you
cannot skip — you must score, then discard. Below ~1% selectivity the funnel inverts.

## The trap

Reaching for a vector database. At this scale the dense leg is **stage 3, not stage 1** — you
cannot compute 10^10 dot products in 50ms and no index makes that free. Lexical retrieval survives
because posting-list intersection is sublinear in a way full-corpus ANN is not.

comments.body:
Marking this, with the rubric and the two answers that separate candidates.

## How it is scored

| Signal | Weak | Strong |
|---|---|---|
| **Staging** | One retrieval step, then rerank | Names the funnel and the order of magnitude at each stage |
| **Constants** | "It's logarithmic" | Names what the big-O hides — cache lines, decode cost, round trips |
| **Filters** | An afterthought | Knows filters break WAND pruning, and at what selectivity |
| **Honesty** | Confident numbers | "I would measure this; here is roughly what I expect and why" |

## The two answers that decide it

**1 · "The dense leg cannot be stage one at this scale."** Most candidates put the vector index
first because that is what tutorials do. Saying why it cannot be — and that lexical intersection is
sublinear in a way full-corpus ANN is not — is the clearest signal available in this round.

**2 · Naming the filtered-recall number.** ANN benchmarks almost never filter; production always
does. *"I would want recall against exhaustive search at 1% filter selectivity, and I would expect
it to be bad"* is a sentence almost nobody says, and it is the whole gap between published numbers
and production behaviour.

## In this repository, at one ten-millionth of the scale

[Issue #2](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/issues/2) is the same failure at 2,430 chunks: a graph with no long-range links
where `recall@20 = 0.00` at `ef=64`. Same mechanism, visible on a laptop, and the derivation is
[here](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/blob/main/docs/30-learning/interview-prep/01-mathematical-foundations/navigable-small-world.md).

**The scale changes the constants. It does not change which thing breaks.**
